title: How long do roofs, HVAC and water heaters last in a rental?
description: Typical lifespans for the big-ticket systems in a rental property, why your building may not match the average, and how to use the numbers to plan replacements.
body:
Every rental has a handful of systems that will need replacing someday: the roof, the furnace and AC, the water heaters, the appliances, the flooring. The hard part isn't knowing that they'll wear out. It's knowing roughly *when*, so the cost doesn't land as a surprise.

Here are typical lifespans for the systems that matter most, and how to use them.

## Typical lifespans

These are common ranges, in years. Your building may land outside them, and the next section explains why.

### Roofing

- **Asphalt shingle roof:** about 20 to 25
- **Flat or membrane roof:** about 15 to 25
- **Gutters and downspouts:** about 20 to 30

### Heating and cooling

- **Gas furnace:** about 15 to 20
- **Central AC or condenser:** about 12 to 15
- **Heat pump:** about 12 to 15
- **Boiler:** about 20 to 30

### Plumbing

- **Tank water heater:** about 8 to 12
- **Tankless water heater:** about 15 to 20

### Appliances

- **Refrigerator:** about 10 to 15
- **Range or oven:** about 13 to 15
- **Dishwasher:** about 9 to 12
- **Washer and dryer:** about 10 to 13

### Floors and finishes

- **Carpet:** about 5 to 10
- **Luxury vinyl plank:** about 15 to 25
- **Interior paint:** about 3 to 7, often at turnover

The [component lifespan chart](/lifespan) has these and more, with a page for each system.

## Why your building may not match

A lifespan range is an average across a lot of buildings. Yours is one building. A few things push it one way or the other:

- **Climate.** Hot summers are hard on AC units and roofs. Long winters work furnaces harder.
- **Water quality.** Hard water shortens the life of water heaters and dishwashers.
- **Install quality.** A well-installed system with proper venting and drainage tends to outlast a rushed one.
- **Maintenance.** Changing filters, flushing water heaters and clearing gutters really does add years.
- **Tenant turnover.** Frequent move-outs are hard on carpet, paint and appliances.

So treat the range as a starting point, not a promise. If your water heater is 10 years old and the area has hard water, plan as if it's near the end, even though 10 is inside the range.

## How to find the age of what you have

You can't plan without knowing how old things are. A few places to look:

- **Labels and serial numbers.** Most water heaters, furnaces and AC units have a manufacture date printed on the label or encoded in the serial number.
- **Closing documents and inspection reports.** These often list the age or condition of major systems.
- **Receipts and permits.** If a system was replaced, the invoice or permit has the date.
- **Your best estimate.** If none of that exists, an honest guess is better than a blank. You can update it later.

## Turning lifespans into a plan

Once you have an age and a typical lifespan for each system, you can see roughly when each one will come due. Put them on a timeline and two things usually stand out:

1. **Something is closer than you thought.** Often a water heater or an AC unit that's quietly near the end.
2. **Several things line up in the same few years.** Systems installed together tend to wear out together, which can make for one very expensive stretch.

Seeing that ahead of time is the whole point. It gives you years, not days, to set money aside.

If you'd like help with that step, the free [CapEx calculator](/capex-calculator) takes each system's age and cost and lays out a 10-year replacement forecast with a monthly reserve number.

## Keep it current

Lifespans don't change much, but your building does. When you replace something, update its install date. When you get a new quote, update the cost. A once-a-year check keeps the plan honest without much work.

title: How much should you set aside for CapEx on a rental property?
description: Rules of thumb like 5% or 10% of rent are a start, but your roof and HVAC don't know your rent. Here's how to work out a CapEx number from your actual building.
body:
Ask ten landlords how much to set aside for capital expenditures and you'll hear "5% of rent," "10% of rent," "$100 a door," and "whatever's left." All of them can be right for someone. None of them is based on the thing that actually breaks: your building.

This post walks through why the rules of thumb drift, and how to get a monthly CapEx number from the systems you actually own.

## What counts as CapEx

Capital expenditures are the big, occasional replacements that keep a property working: roof, HVAC, water heater, appliances, flooring, windows, siding, paving. They're different from repairs (fixing a leak, replacing a faucet), which come up all the time and usually belong in your maintenance budget.

The problem with CapEx isn't that it's unpredictable. You know a roof will need replacing. The problem is that it arrives in large, lumpy amounts, often years apart, and it's easy to spend the money in between.

## Why percentage-of-rent rules drift

A percentage of rent is easy to use, and for a lot of small portfolios it's a reasonable first guess. But rent and replacement cost aren't connected:

- **Two houses with the same rent can have very different CapEx.** A 1960s house with an old roof and original windows needs far more than a five-year-old build renting for the same amount.
- **Age matters more than rent.** A 15-year-old furnace is closer to the end of its life than a 3-year-old one, whatever the tenant pays.
- **Costs rise faster in some places than rents do.** A percentage set years ago may no longer cover the jobs it was meant for.

So a percentage can leave you over-saving on a newer property and badly under-saving on an older one.

## A better way: one line per system

Instead of starting from rent, start from the building. For each big system, you need three numbers:

1. **What it costs to replace.** A recent quote or invoice is best. A typical range is fine to start.
2. **How long it lasts.** Most components have a typical lifespan. A tank water heater might last around 8 to 12 years, an asphalt shingle roof around 20 to 30. See the [component lifespan chart](/lifespan) for common ranges.
3. **How old yours is.** The install date, or your best guess from an inspection report.

From those, the monthly amount for one system is roughly:

> Replacement cost ÷ months until it's due

### A worked example

Say a duplex has a water heater that cost $1,800 to replace, is expected to last 10 years, and is 6 years old. It's due in about 4 years, or 48 months.

> $1,800 ÷ 48 months ≈ $38 a month

Now do the same for the roof, the furnace, the AC, the appliances and the flooring, and add the lines up. That total is your building's CapEx number, based on what's actually there.

The example numbers are just examples. Use your own costs, because local prices vary a lot.

## Three things that trip people up

**Systems that are already overdue.** If a component is past its typical life, there are no months left to spread the cost over. Treat it as a near-term expense, and keep some cash ready, rather than pretending it will last another decade.

**Everything coming due at once.** Systems installed in the same year tend to wear out in the same few years. A building where the roof, HVAC and water heater were all replaced in 2012 can face a very expensive stretch around the same time. Lay your replacements out on a timeline so you can see the busy years coming.

**Forgetting the small big things.** Appliances, flooring and paint turnovers don't feel like CapEx, but across several units they add up. Give them a line too.

## How to keep it simple

You don't need a perfect model. A list of your major systems with a cost, a lifespan and an age gets you most of the way. Revisit it once a year, update anything you replaced, and adjust costs when you get new quotes.

If you'd like a head start, the free [CapEx calculator](/capex-calculator) turns that list into a 10-year replacement forecast and one monthly reserve number, and the [reserve calculator](/reserve-calculator) gives a quick estimate if you only have a few minutes.

## The short answer

How much should you set aside? Enough to cover each system's replacement by the time it's due. Percentage rules are a fine place to start, but the number that will actually protect you comes from your own roof, HVAC and water heaters.

title: A year-end checklist for small rental property owners
description: December is a good time to look back at your rentals and plan ahead. A short checklist covering replacements, reserves, records and what's coming due next year.
body:
The end of the year is a natural moment to step back from day-to-day landlording and look at the bigger picture. You have a full year of repairs, replacements and receipts to learn from, and a new year to plan for.

Here's a checklist you can work through in an afternoon. It's written for owners with a handful of units up to a few dozen, but most of it applies at any size.

## 1. List what you replaced this year

Go through the year and write down every major replacement: a roof, a furnace, a water heater, appliances, flooring.

For each one, note:

- **What it was** and which property or unit.
- **When** it was replaced.
- **What it cost**, all in, including labor and disposal.

This list does two things. It updates your records with new install dates, which resets the clock on those systems. And it gives you real local costs to plan with next time, which are much better than national averages.

## 2. Update ages and conditions

For anything you didn't replace, add a year to its age. Then take a quick look at the big systems if you can:

- Any signs the roof is aging, like curling shingles or granules in the gutters?
- Did the AC struggle this summer, or the furnace this winter?
- Any water heaters showing rust or small leaks?

Condition notes help you decide which systems might come due early.

## 3. See what's due next year

With updated ages, look at which systems are at or near the end of their typical lifespan. The [component lifespan chart](/lifespan) has common ranges if you need them.

Make a short list of what's likely in the next 12 months and roughly what each would cost. This is the list that should drive your reserve planning, not a percentage of rent.

## 4. Check your reserves

Compare what you have set aside for capital expenses with what's coming due:

- **Is the balance enough** to cover next year's likely replacements?
- **Did you spend more than you saved** this year? If so, why?
- **Is a big year coming** in the next three to five years, when several systems line up?

If the numbers don't line up, now is the time to adjust your monthly set-aside. A small increase starting in January is much easier than a scramble in July. The [reserve calculator](/reserve-calculator) gives a quick estimate if you want a starting point.

## 5. Gather your records

Pull together the paperwork you'll need for taxes and for your own planning:

- Receipts and invoices for repairs and replacements.
- Rent rolls and income for each property.
- Insurance policies and any claims.
- Contracts with vendors and property managers.

Keep replacements separate from ordinary repairs. Your tax preparer will want to know which is which, and the difference matters for your own planning too.

## 6. Plan the work you can schedule

Some replacements don't have to wait for a failure. If a system is clearly near the end, replacing it on your own schedule is usually cheaper and less disruptive than an emergency call.

- **Book off-season work early.** AC work is easier to schedule in the spring, roofing in drier months, furnace work before the cold.
- **Time it with turnover.** Flooring, paint and appliances are easiest to replace between tenants.
- **Get quotes now** for anything big you expect next year.

## 7. Write down one lesson

Finish with one sentence about what you'd do differently. Maybe it's "start tracking water heater ages," "raise the monthly reserve," or "get two quotes for anything over a set amount." One lesson a year adds up.

## Keep it simple

None of this needs special software. A spreadsheet with one row per system, its age, its expected life and its replacement cost gets you most of the way. If you'd like a head start, there's a free [CapEx spreadsheet template](/capex-spreadsheet-template) you can download and fill in.
